p.src: Now Zhang Fei asked Yan Yan for a plan. Yan Yan said, “From here to Luo Castle, every fortified pass is under my command; all the government troops there are under my control. Moved by your kindness, General, and having no other way to repay it, I shall lead the vanguard and summon the defenders everywhere we go to come out and surrender.” Zhang Fei thanked him profusely. Thus Yan Yan went ahead as vanguard, with Zhang Fei leading the army behind him. Every place they reached was under Yan Yan’s authority, and he summoned all its defenders to surrender. To any who hesitated, Yan Yan said, “Even I have surrendered—how much more should you?” Thereafter all submitted at the mere sight of them, and not a single battle was fought.

p.src: Meanwhile, Kongming had already reported the date of departure to Xuande and ordered everyone to assemble at Luo Castle. Xuande consulted his officers: “Kongming and Yide are advancing into the Riverlands by two separate routes. They will meet at Luo Castle, and together we shall enter Chengdu. Their forces by water and land, with boats and wagons, set out on the twentieth day of the seventh month; by now they should be nearly here. We may now advance.” Huang Zhong said, “Zhang Ren comes daily to challenge us. Seeing no one emerge from the city, his army has grown lax and makes no preparations. Dividing our troops tonight to raid his camp will serve us better than fighting in broad daylight.” Xuande accepted his proposal and ordered Huang Zhong to lead a force on the left and Wei Yan one on the right. Xuande himself took the center. That night, at the second watch, all three forces set out together. Zhang Ren had indeed made no preparations. The Han troops poured into the main camp and set it ablaze, sending fierce flames soaring into the sky. The Shu troops fled and hurried through the night to report at Luo Castle, whose soldiers came out to receive them within. Xuande returned to the central route and encamped; the next day he led his army straight to Luo Castle, surrounded it, and attacked. Zhang Ren held his troops within and would not come out. On the fourth day of the assault, Xuande personally led a force against the west gate and ordered Huang Zhong and Wei Yan to attack the east gate, leaving the south and north gates open for enemy troops to pass. The reason was that the whole area by the south gate consisted of mountain paths, while the Fu River lay by the north gate, and so neither was encircled.

p.src: Zhang Ren saw Xuande riding back and forth outside the west gate, directing the assault. From the hour of the dragon until the hour of the goat, his men and horses gradually wearied. Zhang Ren ordered the two generals Wu Lan and Lei Tong to lead troops out of the north gate, circle to the east gate, and engage Huang Zhong and Wei Yan; he himself led a force out of the south gate, circled to the west gate, and went directly against Xuande. Within the city, every available militiaman was sent onto the walls to beat drums and raise supporting shouts.

p.src: Now when Xuande saw the red sun sinking in the west, he ordered the rear ranks to withdraw first. As his soldiers turned back, a great shout arose from the walls and troops burst out through the south gate. Zhang Ren drove straight into the army to seize Xuande. Xuande’s army fell into complete disorder. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan were meanwhile held at bay by Wu Lan and Lei Tong, so neither side of Xuande’s army could aid the other. Unable to withstand Zhang Ren, Xuande wheeled his horse and fled along a secluded mountain path. Zhang Ren pursued from behind and was on the point of overtaking him. Xuande was alone with a single horse, while Zhang Ren came after him with several riders.

p.src: Xuande was whipping his horse onward with all his strength when suddenly a body of troops charged out onto the mountain road. From horseback Xuande cried in despair, “An ambush ahead and pursuers behind—Heaven means my death!” But the great general at the head of the approaching force proved to be Zhang Fei. It happened that Zhang Fei and Yan Yan were approaching along that very road. Seeing dust rise, they knew a battle with the Riverlands troops was underway. Zhang Fei charged ahead, met Zhang Ren squarely, and at once engaged him. After they had fought more than ten bouts, Yan Yan came up from behind with his troops in a great advance. Zhang Ren swiftly turned back. Zhang Fei pursued him all the way to the foot of the walls. Zhang Ren retreated into the city, and the drawbridge was raised.

p.src: Zhang Fei returned to Xuande and said, “The Military Adviser is coming upriver, yet he has not arrived, while I have stolen the honor of arriving first.” Xuande said, “The mountain roads are steep and perilous. How did you encounter no army blocking your way, but advance unimpeded and arrive here first?” Zhang Fei replied, “The forty-five passes along the road were all overcome through the service of the veteran general Yan Yan; that is why we came the whole way without expending the slightest effort.” He then related from beginning to end how he had honorably released Yan Yan and brought Yan Yan forward to meet Xuande. Xuande thanked him, saying, “Had it not been for you, veteran general, how could my brother have reached this place?” He immediately removed the golden chain mail he was wearing and bestowed it upon him. Yan Yan bowed in thanks. Just as a banquet was being prepared, a scout suddenly returned to report: “Huang Zhong and Wei Yan engaged the Riverlands generals Wu Lan and Lei Tong. Then Wu Yi and Liu Gui led troops out of the city to join the fight and attacked from both sides. Our army could not withstand them, and Generals Wei and Huang were defeated and have fled eastward.” On hearing this, Zhang Fei asked Xuande to divide their troops into two forces and hurry to the rescue. Thus Zhang Fei took the left and Xuande the right, and they charged toward the fighting. Hearing shouts arise behind them, Wu Yi and Liu Gui panicked and withdrew into the city. Wu Lan and Lei Tong, intent only on pursuing Huang Zhong and Wei Yan, found their route of retreat cut off by Xuande and Zhang Fei. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan wheeled their horses and attacked in return. Knowing they could not prevail, Wu Lan and Lei Tong had no choice but to bring their own troops forward and surrender. Xuande accepted their surrender, withdrew his troops, and encamped near the city.

p.src: Now Zhang Ren was deeply troubled by the loss of the two generals. Wu Yi and Liu Gui said, “Our military situation is desperate. Unless we risk everything in a final battle, how can we force the enemy to retreat? On the one hand, send someone to Chengdu to see our lord and urgently request aid; on the other, use a stratagem against the enemy.” Zhang Ren said, “Tomorrow I shall lead a force out to challenge them, feign defeat, and draw them around to the north of the city; then another force will charge out of the city and cut their army in two; in this way we can win.” Wu Yi said, “General Liu shall assist the young lord in defending the city, while I lead the troops that charge out to support the battle.”

p.src: Their arrangement was settled. The next day Zhang Ren led several thousand troops out of the city, waving banners, raising battle cries, and issuing a challenge. Zhang Fei mounted and rode out to meet him. Without exchanging a word, he engaged Zhang Ren. Before they had fought much more than ten bouts, Zhang Ren feigned defeat and fled around the city. Zhang Fei pursued him with all his might. Wu Yi’s force cut him off, while Zhang Ren turned his army back, surrounding Zhang Fei in the heart of the encirclement so that he could neither advance nor retreat. Just when he was at a loss, a body of troops came charging from the riverside. At their head rode a great general, leveling his spear and spurring his horse to engage Wu Yi; in a single bout he captured Wu Yi alive, drove back the enemy, and rescued Zhang Fei. When they looked, they saw it was Zhao Yun. Zhang Fei asked, “Where is the Military Adviser?” Zhao Yun replied, “The Military Adviser has already arrived. I expect he has met our lord by now.” The two men took their captive Wu Yi back to camp. Zhang Ren withdrew through the east gate into the city.

p.src: When Zhang Fei and Zhao Yun returned to camp, they found Kongming, Jian Yong, and Jiang Wan already in the command tent. Zhang Fei dismounted and paid his respects to the Military Adviser. Kongming asked in astonishment, “How did you manage to arrive first?” Xuande recounted in full how Zhang Fei had honorably released Yan Yan. Kongming congratulated him, saying, “That General Zhang could employ strategy is entirely due to my lord’s great good fortune.” Zhao Yun untied Wu Yi and brought him before Xuande. Xuande asked, “Will you surrender?” Wu Yi replied, “Since I have been captured, how could I refuse to surrender?” Xuande was delighted and personally removed his bonds. Kongming asked, “Who is defending the city?” Wu Yi replied, “There are Liu Jiyu’s son Liu Xun and the assisting generals Liu Gui and Zhang Ren. Liu Gui is of little consequence, but Zhang Ren is a native of Shu Commandery and possesses exceptional courage and resourcefulness. He must not be underestimated.” Kongming said, “First we shall capture Zhang Ren, and then take Luo Castle.” He asked, “What is the name of that bridge east of the city?” Wu Yi replied, “Golden Goose Bridge.”

p.src: Kongming rode to the bridge, surveyed the river once around, then returned to camp and summoned Huang Zhong and Wei Yan to receive their orders: “Five or six li south of Jinyan Bridge, both banks are thick with reeds and rushes, making them suitable for an ambush. Wei Yan, take one thousand spearmen and lie in wait on the left; strike only at the mounted commanders. Huang Zhong, take one thousand swordsmen and lie in wait on the right; cut only at the horses beneath them. Once their army is routed, Zhang Ren is certain to flee by the eastern mountain path. Zhang Yide, take one thousand troops and lie in wait there; capture him on the spot.” He also ordered Zhao Yun to lie in ambush north of Jinyan Bridge: “After I lure Zhang Ren across, tear down the bridge. Then draw up your troops on its northern side and make a show of force from afar, so that Zhang Ren will not dare flee north but will retreat southward, straight into our trap.” When all deployments had been settled, Kongming went forth himself to lure the enemy.

p.src: Meanwhile, Liu Zhang sent the two generals Zhuo Ying and Zhang Yi ahead to Luo City to aid in the fighting. Zhang Ren ordered Zhang Yi and Liu Gui to defend the city, while he and Zhuo Ying formed two divisions to drive back the enemy, Zhang Ren leading the van and Zhuo Ying the rear. Kongming led a disorderly, ragged-looking force across Jinyan Bridge and drew up against Zhang Ren. Kongming came forward in a four-wheeled carriage, wearing a silk cap and holding a feather fan, with over a hundred horsemen clustered around him. Pointing his fan at Zhang Ren, he said, “Cao Cao, with a million men, fled at the mere sound of my name. Who are you, then, to dare refuse surrender?”

p.src: Seeing Kongming’s ranks in disorder, Zhang Ren sneered from horseback: “People say Zhuge commands troops like a god, but it seems his fame has no substance!” With a sweep of his spear, he sent officers and soldiers charging forward together. Kongming abandoned his four-wheeled carriage, mounted a horse, and retreated across the bridge. Zhang Ren pursued him from behind. Once he had crossed Jinyan Bridge, he saw Xuande’s troops on the left and Yan Yan’s on the right, both charging toward him. Zhang Ren realized it was a trap and hastily turned his troops back, but the bridge had already been dismantled. He meant to flee north, but saw Zhao Yun’s army drawn up across the river. Not daring to go north, he headed straight south along the river.

p.src: Before he had gone five or six li, he reached a place where reeds grew thick and tangled. Wei Yan’s troops suddenly rose from among the reeds, thrusting wildly with their long spears. Huang Zhong’s force, hidden in the reeds, used their long blades solely to hack at the horses’ legs. All the cavalry fell and were bound and captured. How could the infantry dare advance? Zhang Ren led several dozen horsemen toward the mountain road, only to run straight into Zhang Fei. Just as Zhang Ren was about to turn and flee, Zhang Fei gave a mighty shout. His men surged forward together and took Zhang Ren alive. As it happened, Zhuo Ying, seeing Zhang Ren caught in the trap, had already surrendered before Zhao Yun’s army; thus all were brought to the main camp.

p.src: Xuande rewarded Zhuo Ying, and Zhang Fei brought Zhang Ren before him under guard. Kongming too was seated in the command tent. Xuande said to Zhang Ren, “All the generals of Shu surrender at the mere approach of our army. Why did you not submit sooner?” Zhang Ren glared and cried angrily, “Would a loyal minister ever serve two masters?” Xuande said, “You merely fail to understand the course of Heaven. Surrender, and your life will be spared.” Zhang Ren replied, “If I will not surrender today, neither will I ever surrender hereafter! Kill me at once!” Xuande could not bear to kill him. Zhang Ren raised his voice and hurled fierce abuse. Kongming ordered him executed, thereby preserving his honorable name. A later poet praised him in verse:

p.src: Xuande sighed with grief without cease. He ordered the body gathered up and buried beside Jinyan Bridge as a testament to Zhang Ren’s loyalty. The next day, he ordered Yan Yan, Wu Yi, and the other surrendered generals of Shu to lead the van straight to Luo City, where they cried, “Open the gates quickly and surrender, lest every living soul in the city suffer!” Liu Gui reviled them from within the city. Just as Yan Yan was about to take an arrow and shoot him, a general upon the wall suddenly drew his sword, struck Liu Gui down, opened the gates, and surrendered. Xuande’s forces entered Luo City. Liu Xun escaped through the western gate and fled to Chengdu. Xuande issued proclamations to reassure the people. The man who killed Liu Gui was Zhang Yi, a native of Wuyang.

p.src: Having taken Luo City, Xuande richly rewarded all his generals. Kongming said, “Luo City has fallen, and Chengdu now lies close at hand; I fear only that the outlying commanderies and districts remain unsettled. Let Zhang Yi and Wu Yi accompany Zhao Yun to pacify the Outer River and secure the commanderies and districts under Jiangyang, Qianwei, and the neighboring regions. Let Yan Yan and Zhuo Ying accompany Zhang Fei to pacify the jurisdictions of Baxi and Deyang, appointing officials there to govern and restore peace. Then they are to draw in their troops and reunite at Chengdu.” Zhang Fei and Zhao Yun accepted their orders and each led his troops away. Kongming asked, “What fortified passes lie ahead?” The surrendered generals of Shu replied, “Only Mianzhu is defended by a large force. If Mianzhu is taken, Chengdu will be ours for the taking.” Kongming at once began discussing an advance. Fa Zheng said, “Now that Luo City has fallen, Shu is in peril. My lord wishes to win the people through benevolence and righteousness, so for the present, do not advance. I shall write Liu Zhang a letter explaining the advantages and dangers; he will surrender of his own accord.” Kongming said, “Xiaozhi’s counsel is excellent.” He had the letter written at once and sent a messenger straight to Chengdu.

p.src: Meanwhile, Liu Xun fled back to his father and reported that Luo City had fallen. Alarmed, Liu Zhang assembled his officials to deliberate. The administrative officer Zheng Du offered a plan: “Though Liu Bei is now taking cities and seizing territory, his troops are not very numerous, the people have not yet rallied to him, he relies on grain from the countryside, and his army has no baggage train. We should drive all the people of Baxi and Zitong westward across the Fu River. Burn every granary and all grain in the fields, deepen the moats, raise the ramparts, and wait quietly for him. When he arrives and challenges us, we must not engage. After long finding no provisions—within a hundred days at most—his army will withdraw of itself. Then we may strike while he is vulnerable, and Liu Bei can be captured.” Liu Zhang said, “No. I have heard of resisting an enemy to bring peace to the people, but never of uprooting the people to guard against an enemy. Your proposal is no means of preserving them.” While they were still deliberating, a report came that a letter had arrived from Fa Zheng. Liu Zhang summoned the messenger, who presented the letter. We should drive all the people of Baxi and Zitong westward across the Fu River.
Burn every granary and all grain in the fields, deepen the moats, raise the ramparts, and wait quietly for him.
When he arrives and challenges us, we must not engage. After long finding no provisions—within a hundred days at most—his army will withdraw of itself.
Then we may strike while he is vulnerable, and Liu Bei can be captured.”
Liu Zhang said, “No.
I have heard of resisting an enemy to bring peace to the people, but never of uprooting the people to guard against an enemy.
Your proposal is no means of preserving them.”
While they were still deliberating, a report came that a letter had arrived from Fa Zheng.
Liu Zhang summoned the messenger, who presented the letter. Zhang broke the seal and read it.
Its substance was as follows:

p.src: Liu Zhang flew into a rage, tore the letter to pieces, and cursed: “Fa Zheng is a traitor who sold out his lord to seek advancement, an ingrate who has betrayed all righteousness!” He drove the envoy from the city and immediately sent his wife’s younger brother, Fei Guan, with troops to defend Mianzhu. Fei Guan recommended a man of Nanyang whose surname was Li, personal name Yan, and style Zhengfang, to command the troops alongside him. Thereupon Fei Guan and Li Yan mustered thirty thousand troops and went to defend Mianzhu. Dong He, Administrator of Yizhou, whose style was Youzai and who hailed from Zhijiang in Nan Commandery, submitted a memorial to Liu Zhang requesting permission to seek troops from Hanzhong. Liu Zhang said, “Zhang Lu has been my family’s enemy for generations. How would he be willing to aid me?” Dong He said, “Though he is our enemy, Liu Bei’s army is now at Luo City and the danger is urgent. If the lips perish, the teeth grow cold. Explain the advantages and dangers to him, and he will surely agree.” Liu Zhang then composed a letter and sent an envoy to Hanzhong.

p.src: Now Ma Chao, after his defeat and flight into Qiang territory, had spent more than two years befriending the Qiang forces and capturing the commanderies and counties of Longxi. Wherever he went, all surrendered to him; only Ji could not be taken. Wei Kang, the Inspector, repeatedly sent men to seek aid from Xiahou Yuan. But without orders from Cao Cao, Xiahou Yuan dared not move his troops. Seeing that no relief force was coming, Wei Kang consulted his officers: “We may as well surrender to Ma Chao.” The Adjutant Yang Fu tearfully remonstrated: “Ma Chao and his kind are traitors to their lord. How can we surrender to them?” Wei Kang said, “With matters come to this pass, what are we waiting for if not to surrender?” Yang Fu pleaded bitterly, but Wei Kang would not listen. Wei Kang threw the city gates wide open and surrendered to Ma Chao. Ma Chao said furiously, “You surrender now only because you are desperate, not from true sincerity!” He beheaded Wei Kang and more than forty others, sparing not one. Someone said, “Yang Fu urged Wei Kang not to surrender. He should be beheaded.” Ma Chao replied, “This man remained true to righteousness. He must not be killed.” He again employed Yang Fu as an adjutant. Yang Fu recommended Liang Kuan and Zhao Qu, and Ma Chao appointed both as military officers. Yang Fu told Ma Chao, “My wife has died in Lintao. I beg two months’ leave to return and bury her, after which I shall come straight back.”

p.src: Ma Chao granted his request. Passing through Licheng, Yang Fu went to see Jiang Xu, General Who Pacifies the Yi. Jiang Xu and Yang Fu were cousins through their fathers’ sisters. Jiang Xu’s mother was Yang Fu’s aunt and was then already eighty-two years old. That day Yang Fu entered Jiang Xu’s inner residence, bowed before his aunt, and wept as he told her: “I defended the city but could not preserve it; my lord perished, yet I could not die with him. For shame, I have no face to meet you. Ma Chao rebelled against his lord and wantonly murdered the governor; throughout the province, every scholar and commoner hates him. Yet now, Cousin, you sit secure in Licheng without the least thought of punishing the traitor. Is this how a subject should behave?” When he finished speaking, his tears ran blood. Hearing this, Jiang Xu’s mother summoned her son and rebuked him: “That Governor Wei was murdered is also your fault. Then she said to Yang Fu, “But you have surrendered to the man and receive his stipend. Why have you now conceived the thought of attacking him?” Yang Fu replied, “I followed the traitor only to preserve what remained of my life and avenge my lord.” Jiang Xu said, “Ma Chao is a valiant warrior. It will be difficult to plot against him in haste.” Yang Fu said, “He has courage but no strategy, so he is easy to overcome. I have already made secret arrangements with Liang Kuan and Zhao Qu. If you will raise troops, they are certain to respond from within.” Jiang Xu’s mother said, “If you do not act at once, when will you? Who does not die? To die for loyalty and righteousness is to die in one’s proper place. Do not let concern for me weigh upon you. If you will not heed Yishan’s words, I shall die first and put an end to your concern for me.”

p.src: Jiang Xu then conferred with Yin Feng and Zhao Ang, colonels who commanded troops. As it happened, Zhao Ang’s son Zhao Yue was then serving under Ma Chao as a lieutenant general. Zhao Ang gave his assent that day, then returned and told his wife, Lady Wang: “Today I met with Jiang Xu, Yang Fu, and Yin Feng to discuss avenging Wei Kang. But our son Zhao Yue now serves Ma Chao. If we raise troops, Ma Chao will surely kill him first. What are we to do?” His wife declared sternly, “To wash away the great shame suffered by one’s lord, one must not begrudge even one’s own life—much less the life of a single son! If you abandon the undertaking out of concern for your son, I shall die first.” Zhao Ang’s resolve was thus fixed. The next day, they raised troops together. Jiang Xu and Yang Fu encamped at Licheng, while Yin Feng and Zhao Ang encamped at Mount Qi. Lady Wang took all her jewelry, funds, and silks and personally went to the army at Mount Qi, where she rewarded the soldiers and encouraged the host.

p.src: When Ma Chao heard that Jiang Xu and Yang Fu had joined Yin Feng and Zhao Ang in raising troops against him, he flew into a rage and immediately beheaded Zhao Yue; then he ordered Pang De and Ma Dai to muster every soldier and horse and charge toward Licheng. Jiang Xu and Yang Fu led their forces out to meet them. When the two battle lines were formed, Yang Fu and Jiang Xu rode forth in white robes and shouted abuse: “Faithless traitor who rebelled against his lord!” Ma Chao charged at them in fury, and the two armies fell into a confused battle. Jiang Xu and Yang Fu were no match for Ma Chao; they suffered a crushing defeat and fled. Ma Chao drove his troops after them. Suddenly shouts arose behind him as Yin Feng and Zhao Ang came charging in. Ma Chao hastily turned back, but now he was attacked from both sides, unable to attend to front and rear at once. In the midst of the fighting, a great host came charging in from the flank. It was Xiahou Yuan, who had received Cao Cao’s military order and was leading an army to destroy Ma Chao. How could Ma Chao withstand armies attacking by three routes? Utterly defeated, he fled back through the whole night. By dawn he reached Ji and called for the gate to be opened, but a shower of arrows came down from the walls. Liang Kuan and Zhao Qu stood atop the wall reviling Ma Chao. They cut down Ma Chao’s wife, Lady Yang, with a single stroke and cast her body from the wall; then they brought out Ma Chao’s three young sons and more than ten of his closest kin and, striking each one down with a single blow, hacked them to pieces and hurled them from the wall.

p.src: Grief choked Ma Chao’s breast, and he nearly fell from his horse. Behind him, Xiahou Yuan was leading his army in pursuit. Seeing the enemy’s overwhelming strength, Ma Chao dared not linger in battle. With Pang De and Ma Dai, he cut open a path and escaped. Ahead, he again encountered Jiang Xu and Yang Fu and fought another engagement; after breaking through, he ran into Yin Feng and Zhao Ang and fought yet another battle. Scattered and broken, with only fifty or sixty riders left, they fled through the night. Around the fourth watch, they reached the foot of Licheng. The gatekeepers assumed Jiang Xu’s troops were returning and threw the gates wide to admit them. Beginning at the southern gate, Ma Chao slaughtered every commoner in the city. Reaching Jiang Xu’s residence, he had the old mother dragged out. She showed not the least fear, but pointed at Ma Chao and bitterly reviled him. Ma Chao flew into a rage. He took up his own sword and killed her. Every member of the households of Yin Feng and Zhao Ang, old and young alike, was also killed by Ma Chao. Zhao Ang’s wife, Lady Wang, escaped the calamity because she was with the army.

p.src: The next day, Xiahou Yuan’s great army arrived. Ma Chao abandoned the city, fought his way out, and fled westward. Before he had gone twenty li, he found an army drawn up ahead, with Yang Fu at its head. Ma Chao ground his teeth in hatred, spurred his horse forward, leveled his spear, and thrust at him. Yang Fu’s seven kinsmen all came forward to aid him in battle. Ma Dai and Pang De held off the troops to the rear. All seven of Yang Fu’s kinsmen were slain by Ma Chao. Yang Fu himself suffered five spear wounds, yet still fought desperately on. When Xiahou Yuan’s great army came up from behind, Ma Chao finally fled. Only Pang De, Ma Dai, and six or seven riders followed him. Xiahou Yuan personally pacified the people of the western provinces, ordered Jiang Xu and the others to defend separate posts, and had Yang Fu conveyed by cart to the capital Xu to appear before Cao Cao. Cao Cao enfeoffed Yang Fu as a Marquis Within the Passes. Yang Fu declined, saying, “I achieved nothing in resisting the calamity, nor did I uphold the honor of dying in it. By law I deserve execution. With what face could I accept office?” Cao Cao admired him for this and in the end conferred the rank upon him.

p.src: Meanwhile, Ma Chao consulted with Pang De and Ma Dai, and they went straight to Hanzhong to seek refuge with Zhang Lu. Zhang Lu was delighted. Believing that with Ma Chao he could swallow up Yizhou in the west and resist Cao Cao in the east, he discussed giving his daughter to Ma Chao in marriage. The general Yang Bo remonstrated: “The terrible fate that befell Ma Chao’s wife and children was all a calamity brought upon them by Ma Chao himself. How can you, my lord, give him your daughter?” Zhang Lu heeded his words and abandoned the proposal to take Ma Chao as his son-in-law. Someone told Ma Chao what Yang Bo had said. Ma Chao was enraged and conceived the desire to kill Yang Bo. When Yang Bo learned of this, he consulted his elder brother Yang Song, and they too formed designs against Ma Chao.

Huang Quan first went to see Yang Song and said, “The eastern and western Riverlands are truly as interdependent as lips and teeth. If the western Riverland falls, the eastern Riverland will be hard pressed to preserve itself. If you will come to our aid now, we shall reward you with twenty prefectures.” Yang Song was overjoyed. He immediately brought Huang Quan before Zhang Lu, explained how the two lands depended upon each other, and added that twenty prefectures would be offered in recompense.
